<reason>Side B won by persuasively explaining why static unit prices fail to interrupt habitual shopping and by neutralizing Side A's operational objections. While Side A raised smart technical questions about product continuity and recipe changes, Side B's symmetry principle—that if a store or app links two barcodes tightly enough to slot the smaller pack into a customer's "buy again" cart, it can use that same link to flag a weight drop—effectively resolved the feasibility clash. Side B also capitalized decisively on Side A's admission that badges would push brands toward visible headline price hikes.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B3.2], [B4.5]-[B4.6], and [B5.3], Side B turned Side A's claim that badges would merely cause manufacturers to "simply raise headline prices" [A2.5] into proof that the mandate works, and then dismantled Side A's pivot that shoppers might prefer smaller packs by noting disclosure informs rather than bans that choice.</best_rebuttal>
